newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-GHEDINA TURNS TABLES ON ALPHAND.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-GHEDINA TURNS TABLES ON ALPHAND.

text.p: Kristian Ghedina joined Herbert Plank as the most successful World Cup downhiller in Italian ski history on Saturday with a victory that turned the tables on rival Luc Alphand.

Alphand had himself become the best men's downhill skier in French World Cup history with a triumph - the seventh of his career - in Friday's delayed and shortened race. But he had to settle for second on Saturday behind the Italian.
Alphand still leads Ghedina in the downhill World Cup standings by 220 points to 205.

The bearded Ghedina clocked two minutes 0.28 seconds down the 3.4 km Saslong piste, 0.23 of a second ahead of the Frenchman and 0.37 faster than Josef Strobl -- the only Austrian on the podium in Val Gardena's two races.
It was 27-year-old Ghedina's fifth World Cup downhill success in a career that almost ended in tragedy in 1991 when he spent two days in a coma after a car crash.
It put him alongside the great Plank, who won here in 1977 in circumstances very similar with the Austrians dominating the World Cup.

Plank won in front of Peter Wirnsberger and Franz Klammer while Ghedina's victory was achieved at the expense of an Austrian team that filled the top four places in the season-opening downhill last Sunday at Val d'Isere.
Ghedina said that joining Plank in the record books had always been one of his top objectives.

"Plank was always such a strong skier, battling against the great Austrians," he said. "Now my aims will be to beat his record, to win a gold medal at the Olympics or the world championships and then take Kitzbuehel."
Ironically, Ghedina was one of the Italian downhillers, dubbed the "Italjet" team, who had the least amount of summer training under his belt because of a double knee injury.
"When I feel bad or hurt, I usually go faster," Ghedina joked. "It happened the same in 1990."
He came back from falls and injury in 1990 to win downhills at his native Cortina and at Are in Sweden.
Ghedina said he felt Saturday was going to be his day when he woke up and saw sunshine over the valley after cloud and heavy snow almost forced Friday's race to be cancelled.
The feeling only lasted as far as the hotel door, when fans gathered outside shouted their support as he left.
"The fans were out there shouting 'You're going to win, you're the best' and its hard to concentrate on the race when people are saying those sort of things," Ghedina said.
The Italian found a quiet corner of the bar at the top of the piste near the start hut and managed to concentrate for the 15 minutes or so before he went down 15th.
Alphand had gone immediately before him and looked about to pull off a rare double win in Val Gardena but Ghedina was ahead at the intermediate stage and did not let up.
Norway's Atle Skaardal, second on Friday, thought he had third place sewn up until Strobl went down as the 23rd starter.
World champion Patrick Ortlieb, winner of the last two races here before Friday, finished 20th and Alphand said the big Austrian may have been unsettled by a training fall.
"When you fall it leaves a mark," he said. "The Austrians are still the greatest team but maybe they had a slight loss of confidence today after yesterday's race," he said.
Austrian Hans Knauss was fifth to increase his lead in the overall standings to 371 points, ahead of fellow-Austrian Thomas Sykora on 282 and Norwegian Kjetil-Andre Aamodt on 260.
"I raced because I love downhills so much," said a tired Knauss, winner of a super-G at Val d'Isere on Monday.
Aamodt did not race the second downhill at Val Gardena and his team said he needed rest ahead of Sunday's giant slalom in the nearby Italian resort of Alta Badia.
